questions.q: Under Section 2(20) of the Companies Act 2013, a "company" refers to:
o: Any business run by a sole proprietor
A company incorporated under this Act or any previous company law
Only government-owned enterprises
Only foreign business entities
questions.src: Section 2(20) defines "company" specifically by reference to due incorporation under the Act or prior company law.

questions.q: In Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897), the House of Lords held that a duly incorporated company is:
o: Merely an agent of its subscribers/members
A different, distinct legal person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum
Identical in every legal respect to a partnership
Only recognised as separate if it has more than 100 shareholders
questions.src: Salomon established that a properly incorporated company is a genuinely distinct legal person from its subscribers — the foundation of separate legal entity doctrine.

questions.q: In Salomon's case, the House of Lords held that the MOTIVES behind incorporating a company are:
o: The single most important factor in determining validity
Legally IRRELEVANT, so long as statutory formalities were properly complied with
Grounds for automatic dissolution of the company
Relevant only for tax purposes
questions.src: The Court held motives for incorporation do not affect the company's legal validity once formalities are properly satisfied.

questions.q: "Perpetual Succession," as a characteristic of a company, means that:
o: The company must be dissolved every 10 years
The company's existence is unaffected by changes in membership (death, insolvency, exit of members) until formally wound up
Directors hold office for life
Shares can never be transferred
questions.src: Perpetual succession ensures the company continues regardless of changes among its individual members, until lawfully dissolved.

questions.q: "Lifting the Corporate Veil" refers to courts:
o: Automatically dissolving every company under any dispute
Disregarding the company's separate personality in specific circumstances to hold controlling persons personally liable
Renaming a company without its consent
A routine, frequently-applied procedure with no special threshold
questions.src: Veil-lifting is an exception to Salomon, reserved for genuine misuse/abuse of the corporate structure, not applied routinely.

questions.q: In Vodafone International Holdings v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court:
o: Lifted the corporate veil to levy tax on the transaction
REFUSED to lift the corporate veil, holding separate entity remains the default rule absent clear fraud/sham evidence
Abolished the doctrine of separate legal entity entirely
Ordered the company to be wound up
questions.src: Vodafone illustrates that courts require genuinely compelling evidence of abuse before lifting the veil — legitimate global commercial structuring, even if tax-efficient, is respected.

questions.q: Under Section 339 of the Companies Act (Fraudulent Trading), where business is carried on with intent to defraud creditors during winding up:
o: No consequence attaches to anyone
Courts may declare participating persons personally liable
Only the company itself (not individuals) can ever be liable
The company automatically continues operating normally
questions.src: Section 339 is a statutory ground for lifting the veil, attaching personal liability to those who fraudulently carried on business during winding up.

questions.q: A "One Person Company (OPC)," a genuinely new concept under the Companies Act 2013, allows:
o: Only government entities to incorporate
A SINGLE person to form a company with limited liability protection
Only foreign nationals to incorporate in India
Companies to exist without any legal formalities
questions.src: OPC is a novel structural innovation of the 2013 Act, extending limited liability protection to single-person enterprises.

questions.q: The Memorandum of Association, as distinguished from the Articles of Association, is best described as:
o: A document governing only internal day-to-day management
The company's foundational "charter" defining its fundamental scope/objects, to which the Articles are subordinate
A document that can be freely ignored once the company is incorporated
Identical in legal function to the Articles
questions.src: The Memorandum is the foundational charter defining scope, while Articles (internal management rules) must remain consistent with it.

questions.q: An act by a company genuinely BEYOND the objects specified in its Memorandum is generally considered:
o: Fully valid and binding regardless of the Memorandum
ULTRA VIRES (beyond the company's powers) and void
Automatically ratified by shareholders
Only relevant for tax purposes
questions.src: The ultra vires doctrine protects shareholders/creditors from a company venturing beyond its authorised scope of objects.

questions.q: The Doctrine of Indoor Management protects outsiders dealing with a company by:
o: Requiring them to personally verify every internal board resolution before any transaction
Allowing them to generally ASSUME the company's internal procedural requirements were duly complied with, absent notice to the contrary
Making the outsider automatically liable for the company's debts
Applying only to government-owned companies
questions.src: Indoor Management counterbalances constructive notice of public documents — outsiders need not investigate internal compliance they cannot realistically verify.

questions.q: Under Section 166, a director's duties include acting in GOOD FAITH to promote the company's objects, and:
o: Achieving personal financial gain wherever legally possible
Exercising due and reasonable care, avoiding conflicts of interest, and not achieving undue gain for themselves or associates
Assigning their office freely to any third party
Ignoring the interests of employees and community entirely
questions.src: Section 166 comprehensively codifies fiduciary duties including care/diligence, avoiding conflicts, and prohibiting undue personal gain.

questions.q: In Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd. (1981), the Supreme Court held that directors/controllers must:
o: Act solely in the interest of the controlling shareholder, regardless of minority interests
Act bona fide and in the genuine interests of the company and its members as a whole
Have no fiduciary obligations whatsoever
Always dissolve the company if any dispute arises
questions.src: Needle Industries established that controllers owe genuine fiduciary obligations to the company and ALL members, not merely a controlling shareholder's separate agenda.

questions.q: In Needle Industries, rather than ordering the winding up of a viable, solvent company, the Supreme Court instead ordered:
o: Immediate dissolution with no compensation
A fair-value buyout of the minority shareholders' interests
Complete transfer of the company to the government
No remedy whatsoever
questions.src: The Court preferred a less drastic remedy (fair-value buyout) over winding up, preserving the viable business while protecting minority interests.

questions.q: Under Section 241, a member may apply to the NCLT complaining that the company's affairs:
o: Are always conducted perfectly with no possible complaint
HAVE BEEN or ARE BEING conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, oppressive to members, or prejudicial to company interests
Can only be challenged if the company has already been dissolved
Cannot be challenged by any member under any circumstances
questions.src: Section 241's "have been or are being" language extends to past conduct, not merely continuing/ongoing conduct — a deliberate broadening from the 1956 Act.

questions.q: In Shanti Prasad Jain v. Kalinga Tubes Ltd. (1965), the Supreme Court held that "oppression" requires conduct that is:
o: Any single, isolated disagreement between shareholders
BURDENSOME, HARSH, and WRONGFUL, examined as a continuous course of dealing, not in isolation
Simply a difference of business opinion
Present only if the company has already been dissolved
questions.src: This case set a meaningfully high threshold for oppression, requiring genuinely burdensome and wrongful conduct as part of a continuous pattern.

questions.q: According to Shanti Prasad Jain, a mere BREAKDOWN of mutual confidence between majority and minority shareholders, by itself, is:
o: Always sufficient to establish oppression automatically
INSUFFICIENT unless that lack of confidence itself springs from oppressive conduct in company management
Grounds for automatic criminal prosecution
Irrelevant to any company law proceeding
questions.src: Mere loss of confidence alone does not establish oppression — it must be shown to arise from genuinely oppressive management conduct.

questions.q: Under Section 244, for a company WITH share capital, the numerical threshold for standing to apply under Section 241 is generally:
o: Any single shareholder regardless of shareholding
At least 100 members OR one-tenth of total members (whichever is LESS), or members holding at least 10% of issued share capital
Exactly 50% of all shareholders
Only the company's founding members
questions.src: This is the precise Section 244 threshold formula that must be stated accurately for full marks.

questions.q: The NCLT may WAIVE the Section 244 threshold requirements in appropriate exceptional circumstances, as occurred in:
o: No case has ever seen such a waiver
The high-profile Tata-Mistry (Cyrus Investments v. Tata Sons) dispute
Only cases involving government companies
Cases decided before 1956
questions.src: The NCLAT ruling in the Tata-Mistry matter is the well-known illustration of the Tribunal exercising its waiver power under Section 244.

questions.q: Under Section 242, the NCLT's powers upon finding oppression/mismanagement generally include:
o: Only the power to immediately wind up the company with no other option
Regulating future conduct of company affairs, ordering share purchases, removing directors, or other orders it considers just and equitable
No power to grant any relief whatsoever
Only the power to impose criminal fines
questions.src: Section 242 gives the Tribunal broad, flexible remedial powers, deliberately avoiding winding up wherever a less drastic remedy suffices.

questions.q: "Compulsory Winding Up," as distinguished from "Voluntary Winding Up," is:
o: Always initiated by the company's own members
Ordered BY the Tribunal (NCLT) on specified statutory grounds
A process that no longer exists under Indian law
Only applicable to government companies
questions.src: Compulsory winding up is Tribunal-ordered, distinct from voluntary winding up initiated by the company's own members/creditors.

questions.q: The "Just and Equitable" ground for winding up is illustrated by situations including:
o: Only cases where the company has already ceased all operations
Genuine deadlock in management, failure of the company's substratum/main object, or persistent oppression with no adequate alternative remedy
Only cases involving less than 10 employees
Situations where the company has too many profits
questions.src: These are recognised, illustrative (non-exhaustive) categories where courts have found winding up just and equitable.

questions.q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 has:
o: Had no effect whatsoever on company winding-up procedures
Significantly reshaped the corporate insolvency/winding-up landscape, providing a comprehensive resolution-focused framework
Abolished the NCLT entirely
Applied only to individual (non-corporate) insolvency
questions.src: The IBC 2016 introduced a major, relatively recent legislative shift toward prioritising revival/resolution over straightforward liquidation.

questions.q: On winding up, the general priority of payment typically places WHICH creditors FIRST (to the extent of their security)?
o: Unsecured creditors
Secured creditors
Ordinary shareholders
Preference shareholders always come before any creditor
questions.src: Secured creditors generally rank first (to the extent of their security), ahead of unsecured creditors and members' distributions.

questions.q: An "Independent Director," under the Companies Act 2013, is generally characterised by:
o: Being a close relative of the company's promoter
Meeting specified statutory independence criteria, with no material pecuniary relationship with the company
Having no qualifications whatsoever
Being appointed solely to represent a specific lending bank's interests
questions.src: Independent directors must meet statutory independence standards, strengthening governance objectivity — distinct from nominee directors representing specific institutional interests.
